payload.source_label: At a discontinuity the differential equation fails classically while the integral conservation law continues to hold

contract.statement: This contract is audited only under the explicit user-adopted interpretation, recorded at gates/leveque-finite-volume/artifacts/session-20260908/user-discontinuity-interpretation-20260908.json (SHA-256 b27e7d260e93edcd5408daa8c5d291ba8bfefd9e66a079480ae6b940aa869030). The original source-only contract and its ambiguity remain preserved (SHA-256 2c88b351c531baff65242b876064168d4e45b673ce46619058a1d3bf6dec0ddd). Original source account: For one-dimensional conservation laws, the rate of change of the conserved quantity in a spatial interval equals the flux at its first endpoint minus the flux at its second endpoint (printed p. 4, (1.10)). If the state q and composed flux f(q) are sufficiently smooth, this integral law yields the differential conservation equation (printed p. 4, Section 1.1.2). Interesting solutions can contain discontinuities, and nonlinear conservation laws can develop them even from smooth initial data (printed pp. 4–5, Section 1.1.2). At such a discontinuity, the differential equation does not hold classically, while the integral conservation law remains the fundamental equation that continues to hold for these solutions (printed p. 5, Section 1.1.2). The supplied passage leaves the precise solution class, endpoint conventions, and temporal interpretation of the integral balance unspecified.
assumptions: The setting is a homogeneous conservation law for densities of conserved quantities, with differential form (1.8) and integral form (1.10). [Printed pp. 3–4, Section 1.1 and Section 1.1.1.]
The stated derivation of (1.8) from (1.10) assumes that q and f(q) are sufficiently smooth. [Printed p. 4, Section 1.1.2, first sentence.]
The assertion of classical failure concerns a discontinuity in the solution q. [Printed p. 5, Section 1.1.2, second paragraph.]
The spontaneous development assertion specifically concerns nonlinear conservation laws and allows smooth initial data. [Printed pp. 4–5, Section 1.1.2, paragraph spanning the page break.]

The discontinuity passage discusses solutions of conservation laws, not unrestricted discontinuous functions. This scope is inherited from Section 1.1 and the reference to shock-wave solutions in Section 1.1.2. [Printed pp. 3–5, Sections 1.1–1.1.2.]

The surrounding discussion covers systems as well as scalar equations; there is no scalar-only restriction in the selected passage. [Printed p. 1, q : ℝ × ℝ → ℝᵐ; printed p. 4, 'Each component of q'.]

Detailed derivations and shock-wave solution theory are deferred respectively to Chapter 2 and Chapter 11; the supplied pages give an introductory statement rather than a complete regularity theorem. [Printed p. 4, Section 1.1.2, first sentence; printed p. 5, Section 1.1.2, final sentence.]
Adopted interpretation: Represent conservation at discontinuities by finite rectangle conservation, including the explicit integrability conditions.
Adopted interpretation: The mass-rate identity holds almost everywhere in time for each fixed spatial interval; the null set may depend on the interval.
Adopted interpretation: Classical solutionhood requires spatial state differentiability, so genuine state discontinuity precludes classical solutionhood.
Adopted interpretation: Do not equate classical solutionhood with the existing weaker conservative residual predicate, which only differentiates temporal state and spatial composed flux.

f is the flux function acting on the conserved state q, with vector output compatible with the conservation law. Its precise domain is not separately specified here. [Printed pp. 3–4, (1.8)–(1.9) and the continuation describing f(q).]
x₁ and x₂ are arbitrary spatial endpoints; they appear as fixed limits in the time-differentiated integral. [Printed p. 4, Section 1.1.1, 'for any two points' and (1.10).]
